# Executive summary 

The global economy is continuing to shake off the effects of its worst recession since the end of World War II.  However, as far as copper demand is concerned the recovery has not been universal, with demand in several of the mature economies forecast to decline significantly in 2009.  This particularly applies to demand in Western Europe, the US and Japan where we estimate that consumption will decline this year by ~22%, 21% and 30% respectively.  In contrast demand in China is forecast to grow by a healthy 23% this year, partly offsetting the sharp declines in Western Europe, the US and Japan. Overall we forecast that global refined copper consumption will fall by 5.1% this year to 17.1Mt. 

During the current price cycle, which is projected to run from 2002 to 2009, we forecast that global copper consumption will grow at an average rate of 1.8% p.a. which is below the average annual growth rate in the previous price cycle which ran between 1993 and 2002.  The lower growth will reflect contracting demand in the mature economies, namely Western Europe, North America and Japan. Elsewhere strong growth in the Eastern Bloc is anticipated. 

We now expect base case mine production to increase by 1.5% during 2009 to ~15.8Mt, and production _capability_ by 6.3% in 2010 to 16.8Mt.  Between 2002 and 2009 the average annual growth rate in base case world copper mine production capability (excluding highly probable and probable projects) is forecast to be just 1.8% p.a., including 1

.4% p.a. ex-concentrates and 3.4% p.a from SxEw sources. 

Base case mine production capability is forecast to decline by 1% p.a. between 2009 (inclusive) and 2020 with mine output falling from a peak of ~18.1Mt in 2012 to ~13.8Mt in 2020.  However, note that this rate of decline does exclude our anticipated mine disruption allowance (6% of initial mine production capability forecast) and any price related/market adjustment.  At the same time, demand for additional mine production (including the disruption allowance) to meet increased market requirements for refined metal will create an implied shortfall in mine output of ~0.3Mt/a in 2011, 5.6Mt/a in 2017 and 9.9Mt/a by 2020. 

We now expect base case global copper smelter production to decline by 1% year on year to ~14.1Mt/a in 2009.  In terms of capacity this should increase by 2.6% in 2010 to 17.9Mt and by a further 4% in 2011 to 18.6Mt.  During the forecast period global smelter production capability is expected to increase by 2.4% p.a., rising from 14.2Mt at the end of 2008 to just under 18.9Mt by 2020. 

Our forecast global market surplus for 2009 is ~1.2Mt which is significantly above our previous estimate of a 0.6Mt.  The higher surplus reflects steep downward corrections to a number of our demand forecast following our LME week discussions and subsequent conversations with copper producers and fabricators.  As a consequence, metal stocks, in terms of days of consumption, are forecast to reach 75 days this year, up from our previous forecast of 65 days.  We now expect that cash prices in 2009 will average $5162/t ($2.34/lb), up 4.7% from our previous estimate of $4930/t ($2.25/lb).  The higher price reflects the stronger price environment witnessed during the quarter.

# Demand analysis 

## Overview 

**Global economy beginning to stabilise** The global economy is continuing to shake off the effects of its worst recession since the end of World War II.  The concerted efforts of governments and central banks around the world have successfully stabilised the financial system and prevented the recession from developing into a depression.  However, as far as copper demand is concerned the recovery has not been universal, with demand in several of the mature economies forecast to decline significantly in 2009.  This particularly applies to demand in Western Europe, the US and Japan where we estimate that consumption will decline this year by ~22%, 21% and 30% respectively.  In contrast demand in China is forecast to grow by a healthy 23% this year, partly offsetting the sharp declines in Western Europe, the US and Japan.  Thus we forecast that global refined copper consumption will fall by 5.1% this year to 17.1Mt. 

**Mature economy copper demand forecast to decline for the third consecutive year** Copper demand in the mature economies is forecast to decline by 22.7% this year to just below

5.4Mt, its lowest level, according to our records, which date back to 1976.  Given the severity of the downturn the recovery in copper consumption in the mature economies will be slow.  We expect that 2010 will be a transitional year with demand increasing more strongly in 2011.  Historically, strong first use copper demand growth has occurred 18 months to two years after the low-point in a recession-driven downturn in consumption.  This is because many applications for copper in, for example, the construction sector, tend to be required towards the end of construction projects (plumbing, wiring, decorative items).  Reflecting this, demand in the mature economies is forecast to recover by 2% in 2010, to just under 5.5Mt, before increasing by a more robust 5.8% in 2011 to ~5.8Mt.  However, thereafter demand is expected to decline on an annual basis throughout the forecast period to 2020.  The negative trend reflects the displacement of first-use demand away from the mature economies to the developing economies, especially in China, Mexico, and Vietnam.  In recent years there has been a growing trend of copper semis manufacturers moving their production facilities to areas where production costs (labour, environmental, power etc) are considerably lower.  Prime examples include Mexico and Vietnam where two of China’s largest copper tube producers have recently set up new copper tube mills: Golden Dragon in Mexico and Hailiang in Vietnam.  In addition, increased exports of competitively priced copper products from China, and other developing economies, into the mature economies will impact negatively on the production of copper semi products (from the mature economies) resulting in some production facilities becoming obsolete.  This is already beginning to occur within the wire rod market following the closure of Freeport’s Chicago plant at the end of last year and the forthcoming (official) closure of Nexan’s Chauny wire rod plant in France at the beginning of next year.  Reflecting these growing trends we have lowered significantly our long term first-use demand estimates for the mature economies since our previous Long Term Outlook report.  We now forecast that first-use demand in the mature economies will decline by 4% p.a. during the forecast period, falling from ~6.9Mt at the end of 2008 to ~4.2Mt in 2020  Previously we expected a decline of 2% p.a. with demand falling to ~5.3Mt by 2020. 

**Healthy growth forecast in copper demand in the developing economies** In contrast, we have lifted our long term forecasts for the developing economies and now forecast that demand will grow by 5.9% this year, to 11.7Mt, and by 7.9% and 7.4% in 2010 and 2011 to ~12.7Mt and 13.6Mt respectively.  The strong growth rates largely reflect robust Chinese demand which is expected to increase by 23% this year, 10% in 2010 and 8% in 2011 to ~6.3Mt, 6.9Mt and 7.5Mt respectively.  This growth will be supported by continued investment within the power sector.  Further

**Long term global demand forecast is unchanged** Despite the amendments we have made to our demand forecasts in both the mature and developing economies, overall our long term global demand growth estimate of 3.1% p.a. between 2009 and 2010 is unchanged from our previous Long Term Outlook report.  In the near term, we forecast that global refined copper consumption will fall by 5.1% this year, to 17.1Mt, before recovering by 6% in 2010, to ~18.1Mt, and 6.9% in 2011 to just under 19.4Mt. 

**Demand forecast to grow by 1.8% p.a. during the current price cycle** During the current price cycle, which is projected to run from 2002 to 2009, we forecast that global consumption will grow at an average rate of 1.8% p.a. (see table below) which is below the average annual growth rate in the previous price cycle which ran between 1993 and 2002.  As noted previously the lower growth will reflect contracting demand in the mature economies, namely Western Europe, North America and Japan.  Elsewhere strong growth in the Eastern Bloc is anticipated.  This is particularly true of Russia and China where demand is forecast to rise at an average rate of 7.2% p.a. and 13.8% p.a. respectively.  In Russia the strong increase in refined copper consumption reflects firm production growth in the domestic production of copper wire rod while in China robust growth in the domestic output of both wire rod and copper semi products is responsible.  However, the removal of the Russian 5% export duty on cathodes

earlier this year now means that the incentive to convert cathode into wire rod, which previously was exempt from export duties, has been removed. This change in trade duties is reflected in our forecast of negative growth (-0.5% p.a.) in Russian refined copper consumption during the forecast period 2009-2020. ## China **Robust Chinese demand despite collapse in export demand** The combination of government spending and readily available credit has provided enough fuel for the Chinese economy to overcome the collapse in export demand for Chinese goods. The Chinese government’s $585Bn stimulus package together with a projected $1.46Tn in new bank lending has, according to the World Bank, accounted for 80% of China’s growth this year. Spending on metal intensive areas such as railways construction, roads and public housing, has helped offset the negative impact that the collapse of export markets has had on Chinese copper demand. **Rebound in China’s real estate sector** The Chinese surge in lending has re-invigorated the country’s real-estate sector with developers re-starting work on projects that were placed on hold at the end of last year as well as initiating a swathe of new projects in recent months. The pace of house sales in Beijing reached a record high in November and growth will accelerate in the country’s smaller cities given the easing of residency restrictions that previously made it difficult for rural dwellers to buy property in cities. However, the authorities are also reported to be considering measures to reduce the amount of borrowing by the country’s property developers. ###### **China buildings under construction (3 month moving average – YoY % change)** 60

**Double-digit growth in the production of copper-intensive white goods** Meanwhile the success of the spending vouchers on white goods was noticeable in the latest data from the National Bureau of Statistics, which showed the production of refrigerators, freezers and computers rising annually by 16.7%, 17% and 21% respectively during the first ten months of the year. It was also reported that producers of copper and copper alloy products believed that underlying demand had improved and, more importantly, this was not solely driven by the recent government subsidy programmes. An improvement in general living standards and strong orders from the construction sector were also reported to be responsible. These conditions supported the 28% year on year increase in copper semis output in October, according to the National Bureau of Statistics. For the year-to-date (Jan-Oct) output is up 17% from the corresponding period in 2008. Further increases are expected as new capacity continues to come on line. Zhongse Albetter Albronze Co. recently announced that its new 30kt/a copper tube plant and 40kt/a copper plate and strip project were launched during this month on the 12th . Prior to that Wenzhou Metals Co. commissioned its new 10kt/a copper rod project on the 7th . **Expected recovery in China’s export markets in 2010** Next year, it seems that Chinese exports will once again start to make a positive contribution to Chinese growth. According to the International Monetary Fund (IMF), exports contributed 30% of China’s GDP growth over the period 2001-2008; if investment in capacity linked to exports is included, this figure rises to 60%. In the medium-term, at least, exports will remain important to Chinese copper consumption particularly in the form of copper semi products and copper-containing consumer goods. **Robust growth in Chinese copper demand this year** We forecast that Chinese refined copper consumption will increase by 23% this year to just under 6.3Mt. Supporting this growth is the impact of the stimulus package, readily available credit and ongoing investment within the power sector. In 2010 the gradual recovery of export demand will outweigh any tightening in credit conditions and result in copper consumption growing by 10% to 6.9Mt. By 2011, we forecast that the dissipation of the impact of the stimulus package and this year’s surge in lending will be more than offset by strong demand for Chinese exports which will lift Chinese copper consumption by a further 8% to ~7.5Mt. Throughout the forecast period Chinese refined copper consumption is forecast to grow by 7.5% p.a., rising from 5.1Mt at the end of 2008 to 12.3Mt by 2020. Metals Market Service Long Term Outlook - December 2009 Page 8 of 44 Copper Long-term Outlook **US auto sales may not reach 10M units in 2009** The automotive sector forms one of the keystones of the US manufacturing sector. Therefore the fact that this year’s monthly peak in car and light vehicle production, of 668k units in October, is just 179k units above the 1986-2008 low and 30% below the monthly average, highlights the extent of the weakness in the US automotive sector. Production of cars and light vehicles in the first 11 months of the year totalled 5.2M units, a year on year decline of 37%. With the cash for clunkers party being followed by a sales hangover, sales in November totalled just 747k units, a month-on-month decline of 11% and fractionally lower than the then unprecedented low reached in November 2008. It is possible that total auto sales may not reach the 10M unit level this year following several new record lows being reached thus far this year. If 10M units are not reached then this will be 30% below the levels reached in 2008 and well below the annual average figure of 16.8M units reached over the first seven years of this decade. **No improvement in US construction sector** The US construction sector also remains desperately weak. Worse still, the outlook for the more copper-intensive non-residential construction sector is expected to remain depressed through 2010. According to the American Institute of Architects, its October billings index improved markedly, climbing by 3 points to 46.1. However, while this latest reading is welcome, it would suggest that the US non-residential construction sector will remain weak for at le

ast the first half of 2010 and probably until 2011 given the 5-12 month lead time between architectural billings and the actual start of construction. Nevertheless, one potential source of hope for non-residential construction next year is the additional government spending on infrastructure. Discussions are currently underway in Congress that could result in the release of $35Bn for ‘shovel ready’ projects in February next year. Such investments, if approved, will be a major boost for both copper wire and cable and copper semi products. **Sharp drop in US wire rod production** The extent of the slowdown in construction activity was highlighted by one major US wire rod producer who reported to us recently that production from his plant was expected to decline by 27% (~86kt) this year. Unfortunately production from this plant is solely destined for the construction sector so no improvement is expected until construction activity recovers. The wire rod producer believes that the residential sector has now hit bottom but the commercial sector still has further to fall. He does not expect any recovery in demand for copper wire rod from the construction sector until H2 next year. As a consequence of this his production of copper wire rod is expected to decline by a further 1-2% next year. The sharp decline in wire rod production thus far this year was underlined further by the American Bureau of Metal Statistics who recently reported a 25% (-296kt) drop in the production of copper wire rod in the US during the first nine months of the year from the corresponding period in 2008. **No recovery in copper tube market** The downturn in the US construction sector also continued to impact negatively on demand for copper tube. Wolverine Tube, a major copper tube producer, reported a 25.4% drop in its shipments of copper tube during Q3 from a year earlier. The decline reflected deteriorating demand from the HVAC (Heating Ventilation and Air Conditioner) and the electrical appliance markets. However, on a slightly positive note, Wolverine Tube did report that some of its customers from the industrial HVAC were forecasting an increase in order levels next year. Taking all of the above into account we forecast that US refined copper consumption will decline by 21.2% this year to just above 1.5Mt. **Sharp fall in US demand for copper this year** We forecast that the demand for refined copper consumption in the US will drop by ~21% this year to just above 1.5Mt. in 2010 a small recovery is expected, with demand increasing by 0.8% to ~1.6Mt. Metals Market Service Long Term Outlook - December 2009 Page 9 of 44 Copper Long-term Outlook **Negative growth forecast for US copper demand during 2009-2020** Over the forecast period 2009-2020 we project that US demand for copper will decline by 3% p.a., reflecting structural changes in the global economy which will see manufacturing and semis capacity relocating to lower wage economies, such as Mexico and China. There will also be an increase in the amount of demand satisfied by imports rather than domestic production. By 2020 we forecast that North American consumption will total ~1.4Mt. This will account for ~5.2% of the global total compared with ~11% in 2008. ## Europe **European manufacturing PMI clears 50** In Europe, the impact of the various stimulus packages deployed by the governments of the region have helped place the economy on the road to recovery. The European Union purchasing manager’s index for October climbed above the 50 level for the first time since May 2008 while the services PMI reached 50.28, the first time it has been above 50 since April 2008. Meanwhile, the preliminary PMI estimates for the Eurozone suggest that the region’s manufacturing and services sector continued to expand. **But strong euro could threaten pick up** While government measures have played the main role in stimulating the European economy, improving export demand is now starting to make a contribution, particularly in Germany. European Union exports climbed in month on month terms by 21.9% in September; however, in year on year terms exports are still down by 18.4%. While exports are improving, the appreciation of the euro against the US dollar, Yuan and most other major currencies means that European products are becoming less competitive and this threatens the revival in the sector. **European auto sector reliant on exports** One sector that has become increasingly reliant on exports is the European automotive industry. German car and light vehicle production increased year on year in October despite the end of the government-led incentive programme the previous month. Output was 531k units, down from 534k units in September, but 6.9% higher than a year ago. Sales increased by 18.9% year on year, to 342.2k units. Some of the increase can be attributed to a general recovery in the economy, and also to incentives now being offered by VW and Ford, including interest-free credit and various rebates. Year-to-date output totalled 4.2M units in the ten month period, 19.3% lower than the corresponding period in 2008. Meanwhile total EU25 car sales totalled 1.23M units in October, 11.7% higher year on year, with sales in Western Europe 15.8% higher year on year. The largest gain was in the UK, where car sales increased by 31.6% year on ye

ar reflecting the ongoing cash incentive programme.  According to automotive consultants, J D Power, car production for Western Europe totalled 9M units in the first ten months of the year, a year on year decline of 23%.  The automotive consultants estimate that production in Europe as a whole (including Russia, Ukraine, Kazakhstan and Turkey) totalled 13.1M units, a year on year decline of 19%. 

Despite improving signals from the auto and the manufacturing sector generally, European demand for copper remains extremely weak.  In France cathode demand has fallen sharply following the closure of Nexan’s Chauny wire rod plant since September 17th because of strike action.  Workers are objecting to the company’s decision to close the plant at the beginning of next year.  Our sources indicated that it is now very unlikely that the plant will re-open at all.  The company recently announced that its Lens wire rod plant will take up some of the lost production by increasing its capacity to a 5- day shift, according to our sources.  By doing this the company is hoping to lift production from 165kt to 190-195kt. However, market sources believe that this ramp up in production is questionable because the plant has never operated at this rate before.  Instead, production is more likely to reach between 175-180kt, according to our sources.  Taking the wire rod plant closure into account we now forecast that French refined copper consumption will decline by 36.2% this year to ~240kt, and by a further 23.6% in 2010 to 185kt. 

**Spanish copper demand down sharply** In Spain refined copper demand has fallen significantly during the year and is one of the worst affected European economies.  Deteriorating market conditions reflect the sharp contraction in construction activity.  As a consequence the relatively new La Farga wire rod plant (180kt/a) which came on stream last year is currently running at only 50%, according to our sources.  This is below the plant’s original plans of ramping production up to over 75% of capacity during the first three years of operation.  It was also reported that production from Spain’s other two wire rod plants, Cunext (180kt/a) and SIA (57kt/a), was struggling.  Reflecting this we forecast that Spain’s refined copper consumption will fall by 3.8% this year to 260kt.  Next year a small recovery is anticipated which will see demand increase by 0.8% to 262kt. 

**German copper order levels improve in some areas** In Germany our sources informed us that Aurubis’s order levels fell by 50-55% during the first few months of the year.  This reflected heavy de-stocking by the company’s customers during this time.  However, our sources also informed us that since that time Aurubis’s order levels have recovered.  As a consequence the company is now running at a production capacity rate of between 65-70%.  Despite this improvement we still forecast a 26% decline in German refined copper consumption this year to ~1Mt as demand continues to be

impacted by the downturn in the region’s construction and auto sectors.

**Further deterioration in Italian demand for copper and copper alloy products** Demand for copper wire rod is also weak in Italy, reflecting deteriorating orders from the domestic construction sector.  It was also reported that financial issues are causing additional problems for one particular wire rod producer.  The continued slowdown in the construction sector is also continuing to hamper demand for copper and copper alloy products.  This was highlighted recently when Assomet, Italy’s Non-ferrous National Association, reported a significant decline in the production of copper bars and sections and copper tube during Q3 from a year earlier.  According to the Association, output of copper bars and sections declined by 95.5% year on year while the production of copper tube fell by 26.4%.  Copper products, overall, declined by 9.6%, to 122.8kt, while the output of copper and copper alloy products weakened by 26.4%, to 82.4kt, year on year through to September.  For the first nine months of the year the Association reported a 26.2% annual decline in the production of copper and copper alloy products to 685kt.  With this in mind we forecast a 22% decline in Italian refined copper consumption this year to ~500kt. 

**Rising credit insurance costs may be an issue for European wire rod market next year** A major concern for the wire rod sector next year is rising credit insurance costs.  One wire rod producer explained that during the first two months of next year credit insurance for some wire rod producers is due to expire and they are unlikely to renew it because it is too expensive.  Credit insurance has risen in tandem with rising copper prices and, according to our sources, can add 5 euros/t to the overall price of the copper wire rod.  Nevertheless, in today’s uncertain market it is very difficult to trade without this.  Therefore, if producers do not have it then they will be pushing for much reduced payment terms or even cash in advance.  However, consumers will be looking for extended payment terms meaning that those producers without credit insurance could lose out on market share.  Thus next year could be a very difficult year for some wire rod producers with further closures a possibility. 

**Weak outlook for European demand for copper semis products** European demand for copper and copper alloy products is also expected to remain weak next year.  KME, one of the region’s largest producers of copper and copper alloy products, recently reported that its output in 2010, while recovering from this year’s dire levels, will not reach the levels achieved in 2007 and 2008.  The company expects that production this year will fall by 30% from 2008, while recovering by 10-15% in 2010. # Trends in consumption of secondary copper 

## Scrap definition 

Copper scrap is classified into two general categories called old and new scrap.  New scrap, or manufacturing scrap, is generated during the fabrication of copper products and returned to the mill for reprocessing, or sold, and is not considered a new source of copper supply.  A manufacturer may generate up to 60% of scrap as clippings, trimmings, stampings, borings, and turnings when processing copper and copper-base products into finished articles.  New scrap is termed "run-around" or home scrap (which does not enter the scrap statistics) when it is generated internally at the plant re-using it, or it may be called "purchased return scrap" when returned by a customer from a plant external to that purchasing and re-using it.  Old scrap is generated from worn out, discarded or obsolete copper products and thus, is considered to be a “new” source of supply 

## Scrapping rates 

The availability of _old_ copper scrap is linked to the volume of copper-containing products installed/purchased and their life cycles, or duration.  The life of copper in electrical equipment and machinery averages 30-35 years; in non-electrical machinery, 15 years; in housing, 35-75 years; in transportation, 10 years; in all other sectors, about 10 years.  The average for the industry is estimated to be 15-20 years.  The rate of (old) scrap recovery and its availability to be the market is limited not only by copper's long life, but also by the sensitivity of scrap collection rates to market prices. 

Over the past 20 years, the volume of _new_ copper scrap has not grown in line with industrial consumption of copper because manufacturing efficiencies have improved, leading to as much as a 50% fall in new scrap generation over the period. 

## Scrap usage 

Most old scrap recovered from the market place must be reprocessed either by smelting and refining, or, to a lesser extent, by leaching and electrowinning to form a pure copper product

.  Fire refining in a reverberatory or other furnace may be sufficient for the better grades of scrap.  This latter process uses oxidation, fluxing and reduction, with a refined ingot, wire bar, slab, or billet usually being the end product. 

Certain products, such as brass rod (manufactured using 80-90% scrap) can contain higher amounts of scrap than others while still maintaining product quality tolerance.  Others, such as wire rod, must contain far less impurities (typically 5%) since these could affect the drawability (leading to snapping) of the wire rod in producing wire.  New scrap is readily used by brass and copper tube mills to generate new semi-fabricated forms with little additional treatment. Because minimal clean-up procedures are needed, this type of scrap is commonly called "direct melt", or No.1 scrap.  In general, No. 1 scrap is contained in copper and copper-alloy products, rather than wire rod.  Scrap purchases by brass mills are based primarily on activity levels at the mills and the relative price differential between cathode and No. 1 scrap, rather than the actual copper price.  When business conditions are strong, brass mills have access to large volumes of return scrap.  When manufacturing (and, possibly imports) decline, mills may be forced to increase their cathode purchases. 

Low copper prices over the period 1997-2003 led to a reduction in the availability of smelting and refining grade scrap with a corresponding decline in the processing of this material in countries such the USA and in Europe.  The notable exception has been China where there has been an upward trend in the treatment of smelting and refining grade scrap material.  Economic and environmental considerations have also played a major role, with the cost of environmental compliance often leading to plant closures, particularly in the USA.  This is despite the fact that the cost of recovering one tonne of copper from scrap is approximately half that of recovery through the conventional route (concentratesmelting-refining).  Secondary smelters and ingot markers typically consume the lion's share (90%) of No.2 scrap and most of the auto radiators and red brass scrap.

During 2008 copper produced from scrap (at smelters, refineries and in direct use) was ~7.9Mt, representing 35% of total copper consumed.  Of all scrap consumed 59% went into direct use with smelting and refining absorbing 22% and 19% respectively.

With the exception of silver, copper has the highest electrical conductivity of all the metals. This helps to explain why the principal application for copper wire rod is wire and cable. Wire rod is consumed in five main wire and cable markets which include general and industrial cable, utility power cable, telecommunication cable, other insulated wire and winding wire. In general, wire and cable and copper products are consumed in five broad sectors: construction, electric and electronic products, industrial machinery and equipment, transportation equipment and consumer and general products. Of these, construction is the largest sector for consuming copper, accounting for 32 of total copper consumption. The main wire and cable and copper products consumed in the construction industry include building wire, power cable, copper plumbing and ai

r conditioning tube, copper sheet and alloy products. 

Building wire is the largest of the wire and cable markets, accounting for ~35% of wire rod consumption.  Rising intensity of use, in both the mature and developing economies, will be largely responsible for building wire maintaining this position.  The number of electrical appliances used at home and at the workplace continues to rise, particularly in the mature economies, thereby leading to an increase in the number of power outlets needed per building.  In addition, recent technical issues imply that more copper wire and cable will be needed in the future.  One of these issues, electrical energy efficiency involves using less power to perform a given task by using more or heavier copper conductors.  Finally, good power quality, defined as the uninterrupted, undistorted flow of electricity at the correct voltage, is also helping to drive up the demand for building wire due to higher power quality being achieved by installing additional circuits and heavier wires and cables. 

In contrast to the building and industrial cable market, the power utility market is the smallest of all the wire and cable segments.  However, demand growth for power cable will be supported by both the general recovery in utility investment and the fact that copper, the mainstay of power grids worldwide, still has considerable potential to carry energy better and reduce losses than aluminium. 

Copper tube, accounting for an estimated 15% of global refined copper consumption in 2007, is the largest of the copper product markets.  The two main uses are in plumbing and heating systems and in air conditioners and refrigeration (ACR tube).  The steady proliferation of plumbing amenities in and around the home, particularly as many houses built today within the mature economies have more than one bathroom, are largely responsible for copper plumbing tube demand growth.  Elsewhere, improved living standards in the developing economies, leading to higher demand for air conditioners, continues to boost demand for ACR tube.  This is particularly the case in China and India where improved power supply will lead to a surge in the consumption of air conditioners over the coming years.  In 2007 China produced almost 80M units of (inexpensive) air conditioners which is significantly higher than the ~25M units produced in 2001. Meanwhile in the mature economies, the market is being driven by external factors such as environmental issues, regulatory concerns and social demands for comfort.

However, owing to its high cost, copper telecom cable has remained the preferred link between the main network and consumers.  In addition, the development of the internet and e-mail has further enhanced the role of copper in telecommunications in recent years.  The need for information to be carried quicker along the telecommunication network has led to the introduction of asymmetrical digital subscriber line technology (ADSL).  The ADSL is a dedicated circuit between a home and the telephone company’s central office that uses normal copper telephone lines.  The addition of an ADSL chip to the existing copper network means that users can download files around 15 times faster than an analogue dial-up connection.

The cable carrying voice, computer and television signals is connected to a central hub in the home. ## Industrial Production Outlook 

The recovery in the global industrial economy has gathered momentum through the fourth quarter of 2009, as the significant fiscal and monetary stimulus packages of numerous governments, as well as the inventory cycle, lend a significant boost to industrial production.  However, like the financial crisis of late 2008 and subsequent fallout had the greatest effect on those economies that were most exposed to the global financial system, the emerging recovery from the collapse in output is progressing quicker in those economies which had less exposure. This has given rise to a pattern of winners and losers. 

The recovery in China, India, Brazil and South Korea has been remarkably robust, and industrial production growth in these economies is expected to return to trend levels in early 2010.  However, we do still have some concerns about the quality of recovery in these economies.  On the other end of the spectrum, the recovery in the more developed economies of Europe, the USA and Japan has been much more subdued, and there remain a number of key issues looming that could yet cause the recovery to falter. 

The key risks to the global economic recovery centre on the withdrawal of fiscal and monetary stimulus policies.  Almost without exception, the recoveries we have seen in the world’s major industrial economies, from the underperforming ones of Europe, the USA and Japan, to the powerhouses of Asia, are largely due to unprecedented and significant stimulus measures.  On the whole, these policies have been largely successful.  However, governments cannot afford to take on the burdens of the consumer and private investor indefinitely, and thus fiscal stimulus measures are expected to dry up into the second half of 2010.  Also, the ultra-loose monetary policy and quantitative easing employed by numerous major economies will need to be withdrawn to avoid a rapid rise in inflation. Authorities face a delicate balancing act between fuelling inflation, and withdrawing the monetary stimuli too soon, halting the recovery in its tracks. Wood Mackenzie believes that the chances are greater of a withdrawal too late, rather than too soon.

The outlooks for those economies worse affected by the financial crisis have been tempered, reflecting our view that their recovery will be protracted.
